title: Seven Sugar Cubes
subtitle: Irish Book Awards — Irish Poem of the Year, 2017
epigraph:
On 10th April, 1901, in Massachusetts, Dr. Duncan
MacDougall set out to prove that the human soul had
mass and was measurable.
His findings concluded that the soul weighed 21 grams.
stanzas: When your mother phones to tell you that your father
has died ten thousand miles away, visiting your
emigrant brother, in a different hemisphere, in a
different season, do you wonder if your father’s soul
will be forever left in summer?
Do you grapple
with the journey home of the body of a man you have
known since you were a body in your mother’s body?
Does the news melt into you and cool to the image of
his remains in a Tasmanian Blackwood coffin, in the
body of a crate in the body of a plane? Or do you
place the telephone receiver back on its cradle,
take your car keys, drive the winter miles to your
father’s field, where you know his horses will run to
the rattle, like dice, of seven sugar cubes.
publication: This poem was first published in THE IRISH TIMES, April 2017, and voted by the general public as IRISH POEM OF THE YEAR at the 2017 Irish Book Awards.
description: Exploring the death of her father, grief, emigration, homecoming and family memory.

title: Ford Galaxy
stanzas: It broke the dog’s leg
when you were reversing for me             on the slope at home.
Racing green
it sits for scrap now
on the tow truck.
Majestic as a king
on his lectica
the ratchets click
the blue straps tighten
before the final journey
out the gates
through which it once
first drove
purchased from our savings
when we were told
we were having twins.
Ground-in chocolate, mud, crumbs
infant seats all straps and buckles
the roof rack bars were your horizontal
handles when you’d stand
and, like the Hulk, begin to shake
us when you’d come to say goodbye.
And the strapped-in children would
shout as if they were about to be tipped
out, and when you stopped, their laughter
turned to Do it again! Go on, do it again!
I once knew a woman who drove a convertible:
metallic navy, white leather interior, gloss veneer
fabric, reclining roof.
A thing of vehicular beauty.
When she sold it she never wrote a poem.
description: A nostalgic family poem about memories, children and saying goodbye to a much-loved family car.

title: Cordgrass
stanzas: In the vastness of Scarborough Marsh
the Great Blue Heron patiently waits on one leg.
Orach, Cordgrass and Golden Rod punctuate
the generosity of the four feeding rivers.
Dense stands of rushes and reeds appear as neolithic spears
and pierce the map to re-emerge through the silt of Ireland.
Here, in brackish waters, they are gathered by schoolchildren
and fashioned into a cross - a diamond at its centre, its four

publication: This poem was first published in MAGMA MAGAZINE, (Grassroots Issue, October, 2024)
description: Connecting the landscape of Scarborough Marsh with Irish heritage, St Brigid’s crosses and family memory.

title: Brother
stanzas: Don’t look at the rosemary on the fridge
shelf – it will remind you of the lamb
you cooked yesterday and how you
joked at the notion of posting
next Sunday’s roast Down Under.
Don’t think that staring at a television
screen will fill the void. The Sydney
cricket match on the afternoon sports
bulletin will emulate the scorch
of your dancing coal fire.
Don’t step outside to breathe the frosty air
you might foolishly look up to the sky
and see the ethereal trail of a jumbo jet
oblivious that it and every emigrant ship
has carried fragments of others.
Don’t look at your young son stretched out
colouring his pages with crayons
– it will only remind you of your brother,
six years your junior, of how you walked
the school route with him, his small hand in yours.
publication: This poem was first published in SOUTHWORD in 2012
description: Exploring emigration, family memories, childhood and the enduring bond between siblings.

title: Hypothesis
stanzas: The editor wants to know why
people are killing
themselves. I’ll tell you why –
because they’re part of a revolution
they know nothing
about. Not a revolution with guns
and knives but one in its strictest
physical sense, the revolution
of the geoid, the planet earth.
We might share it with billions
but these days
we are each on our own
as it sits, upturned on its axis,
slowly revolving, shaking off the detritus
until one by one
we cling to the surface
or free-fall into oblivion.
And so we concoct bizarre ways
to dodge our turn –
we are drawn to the oceans to hide
but drown in their deep waters,
we strive to weigh ourselves to the ground,
injecting ourselves like batteries
with liquid lithium.
To defy gravity
we anchor our ankles to balls and chains
or feel the ephemeral
ecstasy of letting
blood from our veins.
While some tie ropes around their necks
as they take their turn,
ready to hang
from the world, like a tarot card I once saw.
publication: This poem was first published in THE STINGING FLY, June 2012
description: A powerful meditation on suicide, mortality, human existence and our place on Earth.

title: Mother’s Developing House
stanzas: You never knew your mother as a photographer
until you found her student darkroom
asbestos roof and windowless –
her very own Developing House
just beyond the coal bunker in grandmother’s garden.
Hidden by the thick midge hedge and twining bines
of honeysuckle, one summer afternoon
you sideslid the rust-crusted bolt
and felt the pelt of old spider web.
Shattered bulbs crunched on the concrete floor
must and pungence of silver bromide
hung in air from the rafters
with her Mamiya camera case.
Clotheslines of pegged prints stretched from wall to wall
drying for years above four trays
in which each latent image was once transformed
to visible, made permanent rendered insensitive to light.
publication: This poem was first published in SPONTANEITY and THE IRISH TIMES in 2017
description: Recalling her mother’s darkroom, photography, a Mamiya camera and childhood discovery.

title: A Call for Stringent Gun Control on the Grounds That Caution Should Rank Above Faith in Your Neighbour’s Judgement
stanzas: Remember your neighbour who mistook a wolf for a dog?
He rescued a pup from a storm not realising it was a whelp.
His trust in the pup was limited because of its strange eyes.
The man paddocked off his garden and locked up the pup at night.
He rescued a pup from a storm not realising it was a whelp.
Each morning the pup had jumped its fence and roamed.
The man paddocked off his garden and locked up the pup at night.
During the day the pup placidly lay under cobs of laburnum
blossom.
Each morning the pup had jumped its fence and roamed.
The pup had unusually long legs so the man decided to roof the
paddock.
During the day the pup placidly lay under cobs of laburnum
blossom.
The pup was visibly uncomfortable around all but one human.
The pup had unusually long legs so the man decided to roof the
paddock.
The pup had a straight tail and tufts of hair in its ears.
The pup was visibly uncomfortable around all but one human.
In the moonlight, it struck the man he was housing a wolf.
The pup had a straight tail and tufts of hair in its ears.
Your neighbour’s trust in the pup was limited because of its
lupine eyes.
In the moonlight, it struck the man he was housing a wolf.
Remember your neighbour who mistook a wolf for a dog?
publication: This poem was first published in POETRY MAGAZINE, January, 2020
description: A pantoum published in Poetry Magazine examining caution, judgement, and the wolf at the door.

title: Tempus
stanzas: And on his body I saw,
affixed to his sternum
through the skin of his chest,
the hands of a clock.
Thick black rulers,
Swiss precision
in the cogs of his heart
moving them on.
The spider-leg minute hand
swept with unforgiving speed
circumnavigating his torso,
forward advancing.
Always to his
Right.
No time to look
Left.
Release-valves like fish gills
flapped under his ribs,
letting him breathe out of beat
every now and then.
He would sometimes escape
to pound loudly on the piano
or madly splash paint
at a blank canvas.
publication: This poem was first published in THE LONDON MAGAZINE, February 2021
description: Exploring time, mortality, creativity and the human heart through vivid clockwork imagery.

title: Specks
stanzas: You’d sometimes notice his reading glasses dirtied with
particles of dust smears and specks from putting
them on taking them off his fingerprints at the
corners of each lens.
If he was in deep study of his newspaper you’d often say
Dad, give me your glasses, I’ll clean them for you.
Afterwards he’d be astounded at the clarity settle them
on his face look ahead with fresh eyes. South to his
news he’d declare My God, just like new!
Today, a month since his death you find his spectacles
for the first time, unzip the small padded case
study the brown metallic frames, the folded-in arms,
focus on his fingerprints at the corners of each lens.
publication: This poem was first published in POETRY SALZBURG REVIEW, Issue 39, University of Salzburg, Autumn 2022
description: A moving reflection on her late father’s reading glasses, fingerprints, memory and bereavement.

title: At The Wall Near The Road
stanzas: You’ve left a note for the one you love
told them you’ve scheduled today’s crying
for the riverside that their salad’s in the fridge.
You’ll take the many steep steps downward to the rocky
Salmon Leap then foothold your way down again in the mud
to sit on a ledge over a deep pool in the ravine.
You’ll watch August butterflies look east to the upstream
waterfalls hear their downward onward torrent watch
their mergence with the pool.
Later you’ll stretch back and crane your neck
to study the opposite overhead field –
the one that climbs to meet the sky.
You’ll observe how it’s been carved away by the
unforgiving flow of the river’s many floods.
And you’ll stretch to the left to catch a glimpse
of Colligan Church higher up in the land try to get
sight of its surrounding graveyard where, at the wall
near the road, your father lies buried deep in the
ground far above your head now.
publication: This poem was first published in POETRY SALZBURG REVIEW
description: A reflective Irish poem about grief, landscape, memory and her father in Colligan, Co. Waterford.

title: At the King’s Coronation the talk is of the Weight of his Once-Off Crown
stanzas: My Father was a Buckingham Palace Guard his Bearskin hat
rising to the sky like a giant fur bullet or the
whorl of a gargantuan poppy. It was only in photos
years later that he explained
It was tight-stretched fur over a wicker cage – and that
this huge black Bearskin comprised one and a half
pounds of winter and summer head-weight, the bloodlike
drop of a red hackle feather embedded snugly
in its dense pelt.
And on the ground, his obsidian shoes
reflected the red margins of Coldstream creases
soaring towards a vertical equator
of paired brass buttons on a scarlet tunic.
These days I touch the photo’s metal petals of my
father’s shoulder rose, his sparkling garter star,
his gold chin-chain and his young-sloped nose
until I arrive at his vanished fur-screened eyes.
publication: This poem was first published in THE IRISH TIMES, 14th September, 2024 (Poem of the Week)
description: Reflecting on her father’s time as a Buckingham Palace Guard.

title: Chocolate Advent Calendar
subtitle: For William
stanzas: The 1st of December.
Your 4 year old thumb
aimed at Window One
of your Spiderman Advent Calendar.
It takes a surgeon’s concentration
to bite your lower lip and make that incision
into pre-breakfast-chocolate heaven.
A Christmas star
you place on your tongue, like a soluble cure,
allow it to melt into you, merge with you,
become one.
In the milieu of the school run
it goes unnoticed that you’ve turned all Carpe Diem
and seized the opportunity to unseal
windows 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7.
At your desk, you wait for the day to tick away.
Wisdom, understanding, fortitude
fly over your head like a white dove.
And so, by nightfall, you prove
that, beyond all laws of time,
24 days can be rolled into 1.
publication: This poem was first published in WASHING WINDOWS III: An Anthology of Irish Women Poets (Arlen House, 2021)
description: Capturing childhood excitement, family life and the anticipation of Christmas.

title: The Bulbs He Planted
stanzas: When in June his alliums
surprise you from the soil
it’s as if the spheres
are suspended from above.
He stashed them away
that busy October day
when you forgot to ask
where he was planting.
Now the triumphant globes
link this earth to heaven.
publication: This poem was first published in THE HIGH WINDOW, Autumn, 2021
description: A tender reflection on grief, remembrance and a father’s flowers returning after his death.

title: Morning With Four Children
stanzas: The espresso machine gives its chug chug.
Emily who’s two demands an Easter egg
but it’s breakfast time and despite her begging
the answer’s No! Her argument is dug
into the table with her plastic mug:
What’s the stupid difference? An egg’s an egg!
Five year old John announces Eh guh guh spells egg.
How do you spell HOW DO YOU SPELL? he shrugs.
And as the infant milk heats by degrees
and the twins in their pram unite with a cry
the coffee machine releases a high
cloud of steam, and the glass for the juice
(submerged in deep suds in the sink) is teased
by the gin on the shelf: You’ve more than one youth and
use!
publication: This poem was first published in THE IRISH TIMES, December 1st, 2018 (Poem of the Week)
description: Portraying the humour, noise and everyday chaos of family life with young children.

title: You Have Become the Hand Rub of an Olympian
stanzas: When your ashes return
in a small wooden box
a brass plaque on top
there is no cord
or record of attachment
to anything or anyone.
Somewhere a uterus
is evacuating itself
a mass of patient vessels
surrendering and collapsing
bereft of implantation
their futile existence spent.
If we were to walk
every inch of the earth
or soar to a distant planet
we’d be utterly sure
of one thing now
we’d find nothing
of you except these ashes
not your cadaver
or the bony frame
of your being
not the protrusion
of your dental arcs.
You’ve been reduced
to chalky powder
like the hand rub
of some Olympian
preparing to bar-cling.
If this box should open
one accidental sneeze
might spell the resurgence
of your skin cells, hair
follicles, a glutinous eye
or a femur bone.
Rewinding,
back-tracking
you’ve been redacted
to the nothingness of an atmosphere.
publication: This poem was first published in THE PICKLED BODY POETRY JOURNAL, 2015
description: Exploring cremation, ashes, death, the human body, loss and the physical nature of grief.

title: This Dragonfly Emerges
subtitle: after ‘Dragon-fly’ by Lord Tennyson
stanzas: Today I saw the dragonfly
suspended from catgut in the gallery window
Come from the wells where he did lie,
his willow thorax a double helix of soaked and woven reeds
An inner impulse rent the veil
Of his old husk: from head to tail
to become this knotted composition,
airborne, twig-tailed,
eyes with three hundred and sixty degree vision,
Came out clear plates of sapphire mail.
He dried his wings: like gauze they grew
into giant willow hoops – afresh, anew:
Thro’ crofts and pastures wet with dew
A living flash of light he flew.
publication: With thanks to Ed Hawan, Willow Artist and The Old Market House Gallery, Dungarvan, Co. Waterford. First published in 14 Magazine (Vanguard Editions, UK), 2023
description: Inspired by willow art, nature and the transformation of a dragonfly.

title: Ruminant
stanzas: What happens to a heart after death?
It pounds around the rib cage,
at last leaps through the sternum
into the menacing wood.
Grows a coat of fur, thickening around the neck.
Becomes crepuscular,
cannot bear to be seen.
Crumens beneath its beautiful eyes
secrete waxy tears,
its four-chambered stomach barely taking in sustenance.
From spring on its antlers grow an inch each day,
velvety at first as they emerge
but hardening to woody bone for the anger of the autumn rut.
At times the stag tips back his majestic crown,
a Christ with hands nailed up, he bellows to the heavens,
then sheds his antlers and begins again. And again.
publication: This poem was first published in POETRY MAGAZINE, January, 2020
description: An imaginative meditation on death, grief and transformation through the image of a stag.

title: The Radiographer
epigraph: Hear the buzzhum to catch those ghostly shadows
stanzas: Like a perfume plume
you arrived in the world one Bloomsday –
a button-nosed blonde with a mind of her own.
You slept in a bed for a crib
drank Coca-Cola not infant milk
had a candour at three that was unparalleled;
broke news of death with a jolt of coldness,
opened doors to poets in Decembers
with Too late! They’re dead!
Ate your meals with a mermaid’s dingo hopper,
watched horrors each night before bed,
attuned yourself to the earth’s core,
listened for each murmur, focused on each movement.
Your acuteness
lived up to every meaning of your name
Katie: frank and scientific.
You netted each prize throughout school.
Engineered a loop road to ease congestion,
created flow in one direction
found the radix of each problem
like Röntgen, produced, detected and saw through.
publication: This poem was first published in POETRY IRELAND REVIEW (Edited by Eavan Boland), Issue 122 (2017)
description: A portrait of a radiographer named Katie exploring childhood, science, character and professional life.
